newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish cabinet approves banking privatisation plan.
newsitem.headline: Polish cabinet approves banking privatisation plan.

text.p: The Polish government on Monday approved a plan to reform the banking sector aimed at boosting its capital strength and privatising all the country's major banks by 2000, a government official said.

Wieslaw Federowicz, head of the finance ministry's banking department, said implementation of the plan should pave the way for mergers of financial institutions and bring Polish banks up to international standards.
"The main focus of the programme is to strengthen banks in capital terms which means pursuing various privatisation methods," Federowicz told a news briefing.
"The plan provides for making Polish banks more compatible with European Union standards and fit for the market," he added.

He said that by 2000 Poland should privatise Bank Gospodarki Zywnosciowej SA (BGZ), the country's largest bank but burdened with bad loans, and Powszechna Kasa Oszczednosci BP (PKO) savings bank, which needs to restructure its housing loans portfolio.
Poland would earlier sell off Warsaw-based Powszechny Bank Kredytowy SA (PBK) and Bank Handlowy SA, Wroclaw-based Bank Zachodni and a group of four banks led by Warsaw's Bank Polska Kasa Opieki SA.

Federowicz said the government approved his ministry's plan to sell a majority stake in PBK to a consortium or a strategic investor in the first quarter of next year with a public offering set for late 1997.
He confirmed that Bank Handlowy would be privatised in 1997 and a specific method of the sell-off should be picked by the end of this year, possibly in November.

Federowicz said the decision on how to sell Bank Zachodni was due next year. A detailed plan on how the privatisation of the banking group led by Pekao SA will proceed would most likely be worked out in the third quarter of 1997.

He said the government had yet to decide what to do with treasury stakes in two listed banks -- Bank Przemyslowo-Handlowy, where it has a 47 percent interest, and Polish Development Bank (PBR), in which it holds more than 63 percent.

He said the privatisation plan would not discriminate against foreign investors but the government would still strive to help Polish banks survive further opening of the Polish market to foreign competition. He did not elaborate.
The government and the central bank would continue their cautious policy of granting operation licences to foreign banks until 1999, when the sector would be fully liberalised, he added.
The programme will now be debated in parliament.
